query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Dual-phase high-entropy alloys (HEAs), specifically the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA), exhibit superior tribo-corrosion resistance compared to conventional alloys such as DS2205 duplex stainless steel.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with a dual-phase microstructure composed of a BCC-B2 phase and an FCC-L12 phase.
generation.intervention: Expose the material to a high-temperature, molten salt environment combined with mechanical sliding (tribological) wear conditions.
generation.conditions: Operating temperatures of 450 °C and 650 °C in a molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 salt environment with imposed sliding wear to simulate tribo-corrosion conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The dual-phase microstructure that involves micro-galvanic coupling, where the FCC-L12 phase acts as a protective barrier, enriched in noble elements, which reduces the selective dissolution of the BCC-B2 phase.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature tribo-corrosion conditions, the protective FCC-L12 phase reduces oxidation and limits wear by preventing accelerated phase dissolution. The micro-galvanic coupling between the phases creates a surface layer that mitigates degradation, similar to its behavior in molten salt corrosion tests.
generation.predicted_outcome: The AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA will show significantly reduced tribo-corrosion degradation rates (e.g., lower mass loss, shallower wear tracks) compared to DS2205, analogous to the ~1 mm/year rate observed at 450 °C in molten salt corrosion tests versus ~8 mm/year for DS2205.
generation.baseline: Conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205) under identical high-temperature tribo-corrosion conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is bounded to high-temperature, corrosive molten salt environments coupled with mechanical sliding wear. It may not extend to all forms of tribo-corrosion (e.g., ambient or non-salt environments).
generation.uncertainty: While molten salt corrosion behavior supports the corrosion resistance of the HEA, the combined effects of mechanical wear (tribo-effects) are less explored. The exact quantitative improvement in tribo-corrosion resistance remains uncertain without dedicated wear-corrosion studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare specimens of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA and DS2205. Subject them to a controlled environment at 450 °C and 650 °C with a molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 salt medium while applying standardized sliding wear cycles. Monitor the degradation behavior over time.
measurements: Mass loss and corrosion rate over time
Wear track depth and surface morphology via SEM
Phase and compositional changes by XRD and scanning kelvin probe (SKP)
Electrochemical measurements to gauge corrosion potential differences
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA does not consistently show significantly lower mass loss, shallower wear tracks, and maintained phase integrity (indicative of reduced selective dissolution) compared to DS2205 under identical test conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
